paragraphs.heading: Ice at its greatest
paragraphs.text: The Last Glacial Maximum, or LGM, was the latest time in the Last Glacial Period when ice sheets reached their largest size, between 26,000 and 20,000 years ago. Ice spread over large parts of Asia, northern Europe and northern North America. There are no agreed start and end dates; researchers pick them according to their own criteria and data. In Britain the same cold spell goes by the name Dimlington Stadial, dated from 31,000 to 16,000 years ago.

paragraphs.heading: A colder, lower world
paragraphs.text: Around 21,000 years ago the world's average temperature was about 6 °C colder than today. According to the US Geological Survey, ice that lasted through summer then covered roughly 8% of Earth's surface and 25% of its land. Sea level sat about 125 meters below the 2012 level. For comparison, in 2012 year-round ice covered about 3.1% of the surface and 10.7% of the land.

paragraphs.heading: Water locked away
paragraphs.text: The huge ice sheets held so much water that the sea fell, baring continental shelves, joining land masses and opening wide coastal plains. They also changed how the atmosphere circulated, cooling the northern Pacific and Atlantic so that more clouds formed. Those clouds reflected even more sunlight and deepened the global cooling. Once the ice began to melt, sea level rose abruptly.

paragraphs.heading: Ice needs snow too
paragraphs.text: An ice sheet needs both long-lasting cold and snowfall. That is why East Asia, though about as cold as the ice-covered parts of North America and Europe, stayed free of ice except on high ground. The European ice sheets built large anticyclones above them. The air masses these produced were so dry on reaching Siberia and Manchuria that not enough snow could fall to make glaciers.

paragraphs.heading: Dry and dusty
paragraphs.text: Almost everywhere, the climate of the LGM was cooler and drier than now. Most deserts grew, and the water cycle slowed across most of the globe. Much of the world was cold, dry and hostile, with frequent storms and dusty air. Ice cores show dust levels as much as 20 to 25 times today's, probably because there were fewer plants, stronger winds and less rain to wash the dust out.

paragraphs.heading: Forests shrink
paragraphs.text: In the worst-hit places, such as southern Australia and the Sahel, rainfall may have dropped by up to 90% compared with today. Rainforests shrank widely; in West Africa only a few pockets survived, ringed by tropical grassland. Savanna split the Amazon rainforest into two large blocks. Rainforest stayed largely whole only in Colombia's Chocó region and in Central America, probably thanks to their very heavy rain. In Australia, shifting sand dunes covered half the continent.

paragraphs.heading: Where deserts got wetter
paragraphs.text: There were exceptions to the drying. In what is now the western United States, changes in the jet stream brought heavy rain to places that are desert today. Large lakes filled there, the best known being Lake Bonneville in Utah.
